title: Competency framework vs skills framework
description: A competency framework sets assessable performance standards for a role; a skills framework is a shared skills vocabulary. How they differ and combine.
shortAnswer: A competency framework defines what people in a role must be able to do, to what standard, and how that is shown, combining skills, knowledge, and behavior into assessable performance. A skills framework is a structured vocabulary of discrete skills, often with proficiency levels, used to describe, compare, and plan capability across roles. Competency frameworks set the bar for performance; skills frameworks describe the building blocks.
keyTakeaways: Competencies describe performance to a standard in context; skills describe discrete capabilities that can be combined.
Competency frameworks are usually role specific and assessable; skills frameworks are usually organization or economy wide and descriptive.
Vocational training systems such as Australia's are competency based; national and regional skills taxonomies are skills based.
Regulated roles usually need a competency framework for assurance and benefit from a skills framework for workforce planning.

sections.heading: What is the core difference between a competency framework and a skills framework?

blocks.text: The core difference is purpose: a competency framework specifies required performance that can be assessed, while a skills framework provides a common language for describing capabilities. One is a standard to meet; the other is a vocabulary to describe and compare.

Vocational education shows the competency approach in practice. In Australia, for example, under the 2025 Standards for Registered Training Organisations, the Australian Skills Quality Authority (ASQA) expects assessment systems to determine "what competence looks like based on the unit elements, performance criteria and assessment requirements" of a training product ([ASQA](https://www.asqa.gov.au/for-providers/standards-for-RTOs/practice-guides/quality-area-1-training-and-assessment/assessment-practice-guide)). See [competency framework](/glossary/competency-framework) and [competency based training](/glossary/competency-based-training).

The skills approach is illustrated by national and regional skills taxonomies. Jobs and Skills Australia's National Skills Taxonomy, for example, is described as "a new, evidence-based framework that provides a common language for describing the skills" people gain, develop, and use across education and employment. It builds on the earlier Australian Skills Classification, which organized skills into core competencies, specializt tasks, and technology tools ([Jobs and Skills Australia](https://www.jobsandskills.gov.au/data/national-skills-taxonomy)). In the European Union, the European Commission's ESCO (European Skills, Competences, Qualifications and Occupations) classification plays the same role: it "works as a dictionary, describing, identifying and classifying professional occupations and skills relevant for the EU labour market and education and training" ([European Commission](https://esco.ec.europa.eu/en/about-esco/what-esco)).

blocks.text: Choose a competency framework when you need to decide whether a person is safe and permitted to perform a role; choose a skills framework when you need to understand, compare, or grow capability across a workforce. Regulated organizations typically need the first for assurance and use the second for planning.

items: **Competency framework first** for safety critical, licensed, or customer facing regulated roles, where you must show a regulator that people can do the work. See [how to build a competency framework](/guides/how-to-build-a-competency-framework) and [verification of competency](/glossary/verification-of-competency).
**Skills framework first** for internal mobility, strategic workforce planning, and identifying emerging capability needs across many roles.
**Watch the terminology.** Some organizations call a skills taxonomy a competency framework and the reverse. Judge by whether the framework defines assessable performance standards.

sections.heading: How do competency and skills frameworks work together?

blocks.text: They work together when competencies are built from skills: each competency references the skills and knowledge it draws on, and the skills framework supplies consistent names and levels for them. This lets an organization assess competence role by role while still reporting capability in one shared language.

blocks.text: The same skill (for example written communication) appears in many competencies, which is what makes the skills layer useful for analysis. The competency layer, with its evidence column, is what makes the framework useful for assurance. A [skills matrix](/glossary/skills-matrix) often sits between them as the working record.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models the knowledge and assessment points that sit underneath competencies: the concepts a person must understand, how they relate, and where competence is checked. That structure can be mapped to an organization's existing competency framework or skills taxonomy rather than replacing either.

faqs.q: Is a competency the same as a skill?
faqs.a: No. A skill is a discrete capability, such as data analysis. A competency is the application of skills, knowledge, and behavior to perform a task or role to a defined standard in context. One competency usually draws on several skills.

faqs.q: Does a national skills taxonomy replace competency based training?
faqs.a: No. Skills taxonomies are built to sit alongside competency standards. Jobs and Skills Australia, for example, describes its National Skills Taxonomy as a common language for skills across education and employment, designed to work with existing frameworks, while nationally recognized vocational training there remains competency based under the Standards for RTOs.

faqs.q: Which framework does a regulator want to see?
faqs.a: Regulators generally want evidence that people performing regulated activities are competent. That is easier to show with a competency framework that defines standards and evidence. A skills framework supports the case but rarely proves competence on its own.

faqs.q: Can one framework do both jobs?
faqs.a: Yes, if it is layered: skills with proficiency levels at the base, competencies built from those skills for each role, and assessment criteria attached to each competency. The layering keeps the vocabulary consistent while keeping the assurance standard explicit.
